title: Mamluk Sultanate
summary: In 1250 the mamluks, soldiers of slave origin who served the Ayyubid sultans, overthrew their masters in Egypt. After defeating the Mongols at Ayn Jalut in 1260 they took Syria up to the Euphrates, and in 1291 they captured Acre, ending the Crusader states. Ruled from Cairo first by mainly Qipchaq Turkish and from 1382 by Circassian mamluks, the sultanate was a leading Islamic power until the Ottomans conquered Syria in 1516 and Egypt in 1517.

uncertainty.note: Dating start from the 1250 overthrow of Turan Shah and accession of Aybak (some accounts date Aybak's formal sultanate from 1252); end is marked by the Ottoman conquest of Cairo in 1517.

as_recorded.value: Dynasty that reigned over Egypt from 1250 to 1517

where.modern_name: Cairo, Egypt (Cairo Citadel, fortified administrative seat of the Mamluk Sultanate)
where.historical_name: Qal'at al-Jabal (Citadel of Cairo), Mamluk Sultanate

importance.justification: Stopped the Mongol advance at Ayn Jalut and ended the Crusader states; dominant power of Egypt and Syria for over 250 years (R3 D3 T3 L3).

related.because: The assassination of Ayyubid sultan Turan Shah in May 1250 initiated the mamluk seizure of power and established the sultanate.
The Cairo Citadel on the Muqattam hills functioned as the palace and military headquarters of the Mamluk sultans.
Following the Mongol sack of Baghdad and slaughter of the caliph, the Mamluks invited surviving Abbasids to establish a shadow caliphate in Cairo.
Mamluk sultan al-Ashraf Khalil took Acre in 1291, eliminating the final Crusader stronghold on the Levantine coast.
